one_liner: Tiny CC0 128-bit-state LFSR PRNG in C with jump functions; author measured 3.75x reference mt19937-64.c throughput.
what_it_does: seiran128 is a non-cryptographic 64-bit-output generator with two 64-bit words of state, period 2^128-1 and 1-dimensional equidistribution. seiran128.c provides next(), init(seed) (seeds both words with an LCG step) and jump32/jump64/jump96, the last giving 2^64 non-overlapping subsequences of length 2^64; the README also shows a six-line reentrant next(uint64_t state[2]). It is a plain function API, not a C++ engine class.
how_it_is_fast: The state update is an xorshift/rotate linear (F2) transform in the xoroshiro style (s0 ^ rotl(s1, 29) and s0 ^ (s1 << 9)), and the output scrambler is one add, one multiply by 9, one rotate and one add: rotl((s0 + s1) * 9, 29) + s0. With 16 bytes of state, no 128-bit multiply and no table, each value costs a handful of ALU ops, against MT19937-64's 2,500-byte state (README table).
when_to_use: Games and simulations that want 64-bit outputs from a 16-byte state with no 128-bit multiply or SIMD (portable to any 64-bit integer target; C# and Motoko ports exist)
Replacing mt19937_64 in single-threaded C or C++ code where the exact Mersenne Twister sequence does not matter
Parallel or partitioned simulations that need jump-ahead: jump64() gives 2^64 disjoint streams of 2^64 values each
Projects that need public-domain (CC0) code to paste without attribution
when_not_to_use: Anything security-relevant: the author recovered the full state from three consecutive outputs with the Z3 solver in minutes

When you want a generator with outside scrutiny: all PractRand, BigCrush, gjrand and hwd results are the author's, and the README says it has not been investigated by others; xoroshiro128++/xoshiro256** or PCG64DXSM have far more analysis

When raw speed is the only criterion: it ties sfc64 (1.20 vs 1.21 values/ns) in its own table, and in the same author's later .NET 8 table (Culumi README) Seiran at 97.26 ns/KiB trails Shioi (81.97) and SplitMix (91.80) and ties SFC64 (97.80); SIMD generators such as SHISHUA or 8-way xoshiro are much faster for bulk fills
When you need a 32-bit-word variant, float/double helpers or a std::uniform_random_bit_generator class: none are provided
Long-lived dependencies: last commit 2021-01-30 (5 commits), and CC0 gives no patent grant

integration.min_toolchain: C99 (static inline, loop-scoped declarations, inttypes.h); timing used gcc 7.3.0
integration.platforms: any with 64-bit unsigned integers; no architecture-specific instructions
integration.thread_safety: seiran128.c keeps one static global state, so it is not thread-safe; the README's next(uint64_t state[2]) form is reentrant with per-thread state
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces mt19937_64 as a source of 64-bit values, but needs a small wrapper (result_type, min, max, operator()) to work with <random> distributions, and produces a different sequence

gotchas: seiran128.c has a test main() and assertion macros below the generator and exports bare next, init, jump32, jump64 and jump96 symbols; strip the test code and rename or make them static before linking into a project
The all-zero state {0, 0} is forbidden; init() cannot produce it, but custom seeding must avoid it
Each jump runs 128 calls of next() (polynomial jump), so it is cheap but not free, and it overwrites the global state

The speed table's harness (Vigna's harness.c) is not in the repo and its flags are not stated; splitmix at 0.68 values/ns, slower than seiran128 there, is unusual and suggests results are harness-specific
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against Shioi (same author, same 16-byte state) and Culumi (same author, faster but needs SSE4/PCLMUL), pick seiran when you want the plainest portable scalar code with a jump function; SFC64 has no jump function (Stream column '-' in the Culumi table), and xoroshiro128++/xoshiro256** are the better-vetted alternatives at similar speed.
verified_claims_summary: The author ran Vigna's xoshiro harness.c with gcc 7.3.0 (flags not stated) on an Intel Core i7-7700HQ at 2.80 GHz: seiran128 produced 1.20 64-bit values/ns versus 0.32 for the reference mt19937-64.c (3.75x, derived from page data), 0.38 for pcg64_xsh_rr, 0.99 for xoshiro256** and 1.21 for sfc64; std::mt19937_64 itself was not timed.
status_note: Abandoned since January 2021 (the last commit only added a C# port link), but CC0 and a single 131-line C file including its self-test, so trivial to vendor.
